title: Short Stuff: Tick tock goes the Doomsday Clock
summary: Josh and Chuck (sitting in for Jerry and Dave) follow up on the Doomsday Clock, explaining it is a metaphorical clock overseen by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, created in 1947. In January 2025 the second hand was moved to 89 seconds to midnight, the closest ever. They cover the clock's history (7 minutes to midnight in 1947, 17 minutes in 1991 after the Soviet Union dissolved, 2 minutes in 1953), the threats cited by the Bulletin (Ukraine war nuclear risk, Middle East, growing nuclear arsenals, more countries seeking nukes, climate change, biological threats like avian flu, AI in military decision-making, and misinformation/disinformation), and criticisms that the clock is arbitrary and unscientific and that 'if everything's a crisis, nothing's a crisis.' Chuck recommends Josh's podcast series The End of the World with Josh Clark.
topics: The End of the World with Josh Clark

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the short stuff episode, with Chuck and a co-host sitting in; they set up a follow-up to a Doomsday Clock episode that turns out never to have been recorded.

segments.title: What the Doomsday Clock is and its 2025 setting
segments.summary: Josh explains the Doomsday Clock as a metaphorical clock overseen by the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, created in 1947 to track nuclear risk. Chuck notes that on January 28, 2025 the hands moved to 89 seconds to midnight, the closest ever. The hosts discuss whether the clock is reset only yearly.

segments.title: Clock history and the 1991 low-risk setting
segments.summary: Josh recounts that the clock started at seven minutes to midnight in 1947 during the Cold War nuclear buildup, and was furthest from midnight in 1991 at seventeen minutes after the Soviet Union dissolved. Chuck notes the previous closest setting was two minutes to midnight in 1953. Chuck mentions criticism that the clock stokes paranoia but argues it raises awareness. Josh cites Eugene Rabinowitch, the Bulletin's first editor, saying the clock aims to frighten people into rationality.

segments.title: Transition to reasons for the setting
segments.summary: Josh says the Bulletin explains its reasoning for each setting, which now covers issues beyond nuclear risk. The hosts take a break before returning to the specific threats.

segments.title: Digression on Charles Bronson films
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh briefly joke about Charles Bronson, the movie Ten Minutes to Midnight, and the Death Wish films.

segments.title: Nuclear war, climate change and biological threats
segments.summary: Chuck reads from the Bulletin's website: the ongoing war in Ukraine and its nuclear risk, the Middle East potentially drawing in nuclear powers, growing nuclear arsenals reversing earlier cuts, and more countries considering nuclear programs. Climate change is cited as ongoing rising greenhouse gas emissions and extreme weather. Biological risk is raised, including COVID aftermath and expanding avian flu.

segments.title: AI and misinformation as threat multipliers
segments.summary: Josh says the Bulletin cites AI in military decision-making and possible AI control of nuclear arsenals, without focusing on AI as an existential threat itself. Both hosts say misinformation, disinformation and conspiracy theories multiply the other threats by degrading public communication, with AI making deepfakes easier.

segments.title: Criticisms of the Doomsday Clock
segments.summary: Josh explains that the Bulletin's settings reflect discussion among experts rather than measurement, and cites physicist Lawrence Krauss quoted in a New Republic interview saying the number is arbitrary. Josh also quotes National Geographic: 'if everything's a crisis, nothing's a crisis.' Chuck says that is also the world we live in.

segments.title: Plug and sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck recommends Josh's podcast series The End of the World with Josh Clark for a deeper look at existential threats. Josh closes the episode.
